papers.title: Reverse Seam-Carving: Structured Whitespace Preconditioning for Fixed-Die P&R
papers.abstract: At high placement utilization, limited whitespace increases cell displacement during legalization and clock tree synthesis (CTS), degrading routed wirelength. Existing P&R methodologies use uniform density targets or reactive whitespace redistribution, without optimizing whitespace structure before placement. We propose Reverse Seam-Carving (RSC), a pre-placement methodology that redistributes whitespace into core-spanning low-density seams between denser regions, while preserving die area and utilization. We further develop SeamGain, a semi-analytical model that selects the RSC configuration from a single reference run of the uniform flow; one SeamGain-selected run obtains 86% of the best-of-sweep wirelength reduction. In the OpenROAD flow with ASAP7, RSC achieves (maximum, average) post-route wirelength reductions of (27.6%, 15.4%).

papers.title: When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate register-transfer-level (RTL) designs from natural-language specifications. To improve functional correctness, many RTL agents use simulation feedback to guide refinement. However, without a reference testbench, generating one for every initial implementation incurs inference cost even when the RTL is correct. We therefore introduce an adaptive harness that uses a specialized decision model to orchestrate testing, refinement, and candidate selection. It accepts high-scoring initial implementations and generates testbenches for the rest. When further search is needed, the initial score guides repair--regeneration allocation, while defect rankings and simulation feedback guide repair. For final selection, the harness prioritizes test-passing candidates and ranks them using decision-model scores. Across three benchmarks, the harness with DeepSeek improves mean Pass@1 by 5.4--7.1 percentage points over initial implementations and reduces aggregate estimated inference cost by 11.0--14.3% relative to a testbench-guided repair baseline with the same candidate cap.

papers.title: QUISA: A Compact, Flexible and Unified Instruction-Set Coprocessor for QR-UOV Signature
papers.abstract: QR-UOV is a Quotient Ring Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) multivariate quadratic (MQ) signature scheme that has progressed to round-3 of the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) additional signatures call by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Until now, for architectural efficiency and performance trade-offs, QR-UOV has been evaluated only on software platforms and has never been considered on hardware, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). To address this, we are the first to provide a complete QR-UOV hardware implementation through a flexible and unified QUISA coprocessor design, which supports instruction-driven execution for key generation, signing, and verification across all three NIST security levels (SL-I, SL-III, SL-V). The proposed architecture features extensive throughput optimizations by parallelizing key QR-UOV module operations, such as the pseudorandom byte generator, hashing, and rejection sampling. To minimize hardware resources, we propose a modular arithmetic unit with finite-field reduction based on the shift-add folding method. The design introduces a linear system solver for QUISA based on LU decomposition with partial pivoting and a sample solution module, operating over the prime field Fq (q = 127). We comprehensively evaluate QUISA on an Artix-7 FPGA at 80 MHz up to the post-place-and-route stage, utilizing 11,144 slices and 35,248 look-up tables. For higher SL-V security levels, it completes key generation, signing, and verification in 30.4M, 3.8M, and 2.8M clock cycles, respectively.

papers.title: Multi-Order Passive Macromodeling from Layouts via Nested Port-Hamiltonian Learning
papers.abstract: Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).

papers.title: AscendFHE: Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Ascend NPUs
papers.abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption enables cloud servers to run neural networks on encrypted inputs. In CKKS, inference requires costly arithmetic on high-degree polynomials. On Ascend neural processing units, preparing operands and reconstructing intermediate results add to this cost, while limited local memory constrains parallel execution. We present AscendFHE, a CKKS backend that coordinates Ascend's matrix engines and vector cores for bootstrapping and encrypted inference. It uses balanced-byte encoding and exact modular reconstruction to reduce vector work and packs intermediate results in the next operator's input format to avoid redundant transfers. Its two-task pipeline reuses shared buffers after their last read to overlap matrix and vector execution within the local memory budget. On Ascend 910B3, AscendFHE achieves a 4.61$\times$ bootstrapping speedup and 1.59$\times$--2.00$\times$ encrypted-inference speedups across ResNet-20, BERT-base, and Llama 3 8B over our Vector-based Ascend port of Cheddar.

papers.title: LIELLA: Private Edge Adaptation with Photonic Weight Streams
papers.abstract: Although photonic accelerators have shown promise for energy-efficient machine learning inference, privately personalizing large models across multiple edge clients remains difficult under tight memory, precision, and hardware constraints. We present LIELLA, a weight-streaming architecture that enables multiple edge clients to personalize a shared model through compact private adapters. The two proposed photonic adapter architectures accommodate both backpropagation and forward-only optimization while substantially reducing modeled client-side electrical energy consumption compared with electronic adapters. Under simulated hardware noise, clients sharing the same streamed backbone achieve nearly clean accuracy on QNLI and SST-2, even with attojoule-scale optical energy per MAC at each receiver. The architecture also enables hardware-aware adaptation among clients performing the same task, allowing their individual private adapters to achieve further accuracy improvements. For a gigabyte-scale TinyLlama backbone, LIELLA maintains a megabyte-scale inference memory footprint and kilobyte-scale persistent adapter storage per client, while achieving strong performance through forward-only adaptation. These findings further highlight hardware-driven opportunities to develop smaller yet more effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods and more accurate, noise-robust forward-only optimization algorithms.

papers.title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
papers.abstract: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Verilog Code Refinement for Efficient RTL Clock Gating
papers.abstract: RTL clock gating is a popular technique for reducing clock power at the early design stage. Iterative updates of Verilog code, clock-gating inference, and analysis of clock-gating efficiency (CGE) are time-consuming and pose challenges to RTL designers. LLM-assisted automatic refinement of Verilog code for improving CGE is proposed. Since CGE and power depend on switching activity, LLMs generate Idle, Typical, and Peak workloads of the design, one of which is selected by the user as the optimization target. Four LLM clock-gating agents, each given a guideline for a particular clock-gating technique, then sequentially refine the Verilog code, focusing on the registers with low flop-gating efficiency (FGE) under the selected workload. Code updates are accepted only if they are functionally equivalent and reduce post-synthesis power without violating area and timing constraints. Experimental results with five RTL designs show an average FGE improvement of 12.1 percentage points and an average power reduction of 23.6% (up to 59.3%) under the selected workloads, compared to the original Verilog code, outperforming a commercial tool and an LLM baseline, which achieve average power reductions of only 4.1% and 8.6%, respectively.

papers.title: Gossamer: A Utility-Driven Architecture for Constant-Budget KV Cache Compression in Reasoning LLMs
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex reasoning tasks, yet their inference efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the rapid growth of the KV cache. As reasoning contexts extend to hundreds of thousands of tokens, the key-value (KV) cache becomes the dominant contributor to both memory footprint and bandwidth demand, tightly coupling computation with memory utilization and thereby limiting scalability. Existing compression methods, such as quantization and eviction, alleviate capacity pressure but remain purely algorithmic, often introducing additional passes and compute overhead that reduce system efficiency. This paper presents Gossamer, a KV cache compression architecture for reasoning LLMs that bridges the algorithm--system--hardware gap. Gossamer introduces a unified utility-based action framework that dynamically selects compression operations, quantization, merging, or eviction, under a constant KV cache budget. Through cross-domain co-design, we fuse cosine-similarity estimation directly into the attention computation, exploiting idle compute cycles to perform similarity evaluation without latency or bandwidth cost. We call this mechanism Free-Lunch Utilization. This enables real-time, fine-grained KV management with near-constant memory usage and negligible overhead. Under tight memory constraints, Gossamer sustains reasoning quality comparable to uncompressed inference while improving end-to-end throughput by up to 16.7$\times$ over uncompressed baselines, 5.5$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ over the quantization-based Oaken and Ecco, and 1.8$\times$ over the eviction-based R-KV.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Co-Optimization of RTL and Synthesis Algorithms via Bottleneck Analysis
papers.abstract: Post-synthesis power, performance, and area (PPA) depend jointly on the register-transfer-level (RTL) code and the synthesis algorithms. However, the benefits of RTL optimization may be limited by bottlenecks in synthesis algorithms, and vice versa, leaving opportunities for better PPA unexplored by methods that optimize either level alone. In this work, we present a large language model (LLM)-assisted framework for regional co-optimization of RTL and synthesis algorithms via bottleneck analysis. A key insight behind our approach is that RTL structures and the Boolean networks used in synthesis expose complementary opportunities for addressing bottlenecks that lead to suboptimal PPA in different regions of the circuit. Our bottleneck analysis uses a Gaussian process (GP) to assess whether optimizing RTL or synthesis algorithms is more promising for each region. The GP learns from regional graph representations and PPA feedback. Using the GP's predictions and predictive uncertainty, Bayesian optimization (BO) provides guidance that an LLM Router combines with circuit analysis to choose how to address each region's bottlenecks. Self-improving LLM workers then optimize the RTL or synthesis algorithms in their assigned regions, and their regional changes are greedily integrated into the current design configuration. Experiments on 16 RTL designs show average improvements of 103.27% in worst negative slack (WNS), 1.23% in area, and 13.26% in power relative to the initial designs. These improvements exceed those of the strongest baseline for each metric by 47.80, 2.75, and 13.17 percentage points, respectively.

papers.title: Synapse: An HBM-Coordinated HBF Near-Memory Computing Architecture for Pipelined Agentic AI Execution
papers.abstract: During multi-agent video reasoning, model weights and per-agent key-value caches can exceed high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) adds capacity, but agents still wait for GPU execution. Synapse, an HBM-coordinated near-memory computing architecture, overlaps HBF attention and expert execution with GPU computation across agents. It also reduces dispatch delays and unnecessary refreshes. Across three models, Synapse achieves 48.92-66.60% lower end-to-end latency, up to $2.98\times$ throughput, and up to 64.48% lower modeled energy per output token than GPU execution with passive HBF. Wear simulations project 46% longer HBF lifetime than block-wide refresh at equal workload rates.

papers.title: Measuring GPU Memory Traffic on the NVIDIA GB10 Without C2C Telemetry
papers.abstract: The NVIDIA GB10, used in the DGX Spark and in desktop AI systems from several vendors, joins an Arm CPU die and a Blackwell GPU die with NVLink C2C. The GPU has no local memory, so every GPU access that misses in its L2 cache crosses C2C to the LPDDR5X attached to the CPU die. Yet the software on the systems we tested exposes no counter for this traffic. We show that five L2 sector counters of the GPU, sampled every 10 ms through NVIDIA's CUPTI sampling interface by a process that does not attach to the workload, measure GPU memory traffic live and separate copy engine traffic from the read misses and writes of GPU kernels. For large streaming transfers of known size, the counters agree within 0.28% on an Acer GN100 and within 0.005% on a DGX Spark, track the volume moved regardless of how it is split into copies, and exclude data reused in L2. The GPU's SMMU counter, a natural alternative, counts address translations rather than bytes. Applied to an unmodified server, the method shows Mistral 7B decode reading 13.47 GiB per token, the weights it uses plus its key value (KV) cache, at 83% of the memory bandwidth NVIDIA specifies. We release the method as an open source tool.

papers.title: Resource-Aware VLA-MPC Co-Location for Efficient Embodied AI
papers.abstract: Recent advances in embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) have unleashed new potential in many frontiers. Current EAI systems often combine vision-language-action (VLA) inference with high frequency model predictive control (MPC). On mobile GPUs, these workloads are typically serialized, causing control deadline misses. We present Dubot, a framework that automatically schedules VLA inference and MPC on a single mobile GPU. Specifically, Dubot identifies concurrent opportunities and proposes three co-location mechanisms: spatial partitioning, block-level co-location, and intra-block fusion. By leveraging different mechanisms, Dubot enables fine-grained co-location to improve the efficiency of various VLA-MPC operator pairs. Dubot further proposes a co-location optimizer that can determine the optimal co-location schedule under workload dependency, QoS requirements, and hardware-resource constraints. Across representative VLA inference paradigms on NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Thor, Dubot achieves up to 1.4x end-to-end speedup and reduces QoS violations by up to 38%.

papers.title: Making Protocol Effects Explicit: LLM-to-Packet Simulation for Superpod Interconnect Exploration
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the foundation of modern AI services. The rapid growth of LLM sizes and context lengths has exceeded the memory capacity of a single GPU or NPU, requiring model partitioning across devices. However, partitioning models across devices introduces costly communication overhead, driving the need for superpods with large-scale, high-bandwidth, low-latency scale-up fabrics. Exploring superpod designs requires accurate interconnect simulation, as communication latency is jointly determined by link technologies, topologies, and scale-up protocol-stack choices. Latency-bandwidth models estimate communication latency using a startup term and a transfer term derived from message size and effective bandwidth. But they fail to capture contention and protocol effects. Packet-level simulators like ns-3 model routing, queueing, and packet timing, but require protocol-specific LLM-to-packet implementations. This paper presents ProtoBridge, an ns-3-based LLM-to-packet simulator for superpod interconnect exploration. To make protocol effects explicit, ProtoBridge introduces two abstraction layers over ns-3: (1) an operation-to-packet (OTP) layer that captures protocol-specific packet exchanges and dependencies, and (2) a packet-execution (PEX) layer that applies shared packet-level mechanisms to the ns-3 event system. ProtoBridge achieves average latency error of 17.8\% on H200 NVLink4 and 10.3\% on C500 MetaXLink. To enable faster superpod evaluation for further interconnect exploration, we derive a surrogate model that combines OTP parameters with analytical models of PEX mechanisms. The surrogate reduces evaluation time from 2.38$\sim$75.70s to 20.5us per operation. We use ProtoBridge to analyze two emerging superpod designs, scale-up memory pool and co-packaged optics (CPO) interconnects, revealing design insights for future LLM superpod architectures.

papers.title: EdgeALM: An Efficient and Unified Edge Accelerator for Large Audio Language Models via Full-Stack Hardware-Software Co-Design and Agent-Driven Recursive Optimization
papers.abstract: Edge deployment of audio language models (ALMs) is constrained by large model footprints, heterogeneous workloads, and limited software support. This paper presents EdgeALM, an efficient and unified FPGA accelerator for ALMs that combines full-stack hardware-software co-design with agent-driven recursive optimization. An end-to-end ALM compression flow is developed, combining a unified AWQ-style quantizer with modality-conditioned vocabulary pruning. A Conv-Matmul Disaggregation architecture is proposed, with dedicated matrix and convolution engines that operate concurrently on their respective workloads. An Extra-Coarse-Grained ISA is designed to incorporate regular on-chip data movement and execution sequences into compute instructions, reducing software complexity with modest hardware control overhead. Hardware and software recursive loops are introduced for agent-driven full-stack optimization. The proposed EdgeALM is implemented on a single Alveo U50 in an ordinary desktop PC and demonstrates inference on more than 20 models, including ALMs with up to 13B parameters within the 8-GB HBM capacity. It achieves high-throughput audio-to-text inference at up to 169.5 tokens/s and sustains real-time streaming audio-to-audio inference, with 94% bandwidth utilization and 26 W power consumption on average. Standalone ASR, text-only LLM, and TTS models are also well supported, and can be combined in cascades. Compared with state-of-the-art FPGA accelerators (e.g., EdgeLLM), EdgeALM scales to larger models and supports a wider range of inference workloads extended to the audio modality, while achieving higher bandwidth utilization at lower board power and cost.

papers.title: CHIP: Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection. Can OpenAI CLIP Reconstruct Images from the CPU Computational Footprint?
papers.abstract: Image inference on a shared CPU leaves input-dependent traces in software-visible performance counters and execution time. CHIP (Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection) trains a lightweight residual projector on public images to map these measurements into the 768-dimensional visual embedding space of a frozen OpenAI CLIP model. A frozen Stable unCLIP generator uses the projected embeddings to reconstruct recognizable color scenes for held-out inputs. The attack requires no physical probe, candidate image gallery, domain-specific generator, or shared cache, and elapsed time alone retains the signal. We evaluate full-counter, single-counter, and timing-only measurements on Intel Haswell and Sapphire Rapids. The projected embeddings achieve 0.85 ROC AUC for held-out image identification, compared with a 0.50 baseline. Exact-image top-five retrieval reaches 24% on CIFAR-100 and 56% on Unsafe-Diffusion. Across both processors, reconstructions average $1.4\times$ the baseline RGB color-palette overlap and $2.5\times$ the baseline structural similarity.

papers.title: WEPWAWET-CORE: A Hardware-Resident ML-DSA Architecture with Fabric-Generated, Fabric-Sealed Keys for Post-Quantum Avionics
papers.abstract: Spacecraft that exchange commands over crosslinks need quantum-resistant signatures, for which the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA, FIPS 204) is the standard, yet a software signer runs its data-dependent rejection loop, and keeps its key, on cores and memory shared with attitude control and payload processing. This paper shows that for a hardware-assisted signer the cost that matters is not the arithmetic but the number of times the processor crosses into the fabric, and that the boundary which minimizes those crossings is also where the key can be sealed. A gem5-supported analysis of three control granularities over the same kernels shows that only one job per signature, with the whole rejection loop on chip, takes the processor off the critical path. WEPWAWET-CORE realizes that boundary on an XCZU3EG at 300 MHz: a ROM microsequencer runs Sign, Verify, and key generation as three programs over one datapath and a banked scratchpad, and keeps the key, the on-die entropy, and the mask seed off the processor bus. The processor-side cost of a signature falls from over a second under per-kernel control to 0.53 ms, fixed whatever the number of rejections, and the fabric's time per attempt varies by less than 0.1% under a saturating workload. Under NASA JPL's F Prime with attitude-control and imaging loads, two nodes with fabric-generated, ground-certified keys exchanged 3,575 signed frames, every frame was accepted, and no attitude deadline was missed. A cycle profile places the remaining distance to dedicated cores in two serial units.

papers.title: ANOR: Scaling Sparse Attention with a GPU-PNM Computing Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Serving large language models with long contexts requires keeping the key-value (KV) cache of every request, which can exceed GPU memory capacity. Sparse attention reads only a small, query-dependent subset of this cache at each decoding step, yet must retain the full cache because later steps may select other entries. Processing-near-memory (PNM) devices attached through Compute Express Link (CXL) can hold the full cache and compute attention where it resides. Prior GPU-PNM systems for sparse attention are PNM-centric, processing most of the attention on the PNM. As existing CXL-PNM devices provide far less memory bandwidth than GPU HBM, this PNM-centric execution makes the PNM the bottleneck and leaves the GPU idle waiting for attention results. We present ANOR, a GPU-PNM joint acceleration system that exploits the selection locality of sparse attention by computing most of the attention on the GPU from a cache of recently selected entries and processing only the misses on the PNM. As the PNM processes cache misses directly, GPU cache updates can be decoupled from current-step execution. We develop a bounded cache-update policy that limits updates to the point where the hit ratio of later steps saturates, reducing GPU-facing link traffic. We add a small on-chip Early Streaming Buffer (ESB) that captures KV data during PNM attention and streams it to the GPU, avoiding most redundant DRAM reads despite the bandwidth mismatch between PNM memory and the GPU-facing link. We also propose an adaptive cache-factor mechanism that adjusts GPU cache size to the serving load, balancing hit ratio and batch size. Across two models and three long-context agentic workloads, ANOR improves decode throughput by 2.3x over HiSparse and 2.0x over a PNM baseline on average. These results show that PNM is most effective not as the primary attention engine but as a computing tier of the GPU memory hierarchy.

papers.title: Pudding: A Retargetable Compiler for Processing-Using-DRAM Systems
papers.abstract: Processing-Using-DRAM (PUD) architectures exploit the physics of DRAM arrays to perform Boolean operations directly in memory, eliminating the data movement bottleneck in memory-intensive workloads. Several PUD architectures have been recently proposed which differ in their primitive operation sets, row allocation models, and execution metrics. These architectural differences are today hard-coded in emerging PUD-aware compilers, making crossarchitecture reuse impossible. We present a retargetable, end-to-end compilation framework for PUD architectures. The central idea is to make the architecture description a first-class object in the compilation pipeline: retargeting to a new PUD architecture only requires supplying its description. Built upon the MLIR framework, our compiler operates at two coupled levels. At the tensor level, it lowers high-level programs through bit-slicing, mixed-precision assignment, and integer-linear-programming (ILP) based placement to reduce the number of PUD commands and inter-bank data movement. At the logic level, it employs equality saturation to explore Boolean network implementations, with rewrite rules and cost functions derived directly from the architecture description. Evaluated on representative workloads across multiple PUD targets with the same compiler passes, our framework matches (and in several cases surpasses) architecture-specific hand-optimized compilers, while delivering retargetability and extensibility.

papers.title: HLWalk: Modal-Split Random-Walk Thermal Analysis for Heterogeneous 2.5D/3D ICs
papers.abstract: Efficient thermal analysis is essential for accelerating the design of 2.5D/3D ICs. However, existing random-walk thermal solvers can suffer from boundary discretization errors and high computational costs when resolving fine-scale structures such as through-silicon vias (TSVs). To address these challenges, we propose HLWalk, an efficient random-walk thermal solver for heterogeneous 2.5D/3D ICs. We introduce local boundary integral reconstruction to eliminate discretization errors in local-time-based boundary treatments. To accelerate boundary preprocessing, we employ modal splitting: low-order modes are computed deterministically, while Monte Carlo sampling estimates only the residual. We further develop scale-aware random-walk transport to efficiently resolve fine-scale structures without requiring fine discretization throughout the domain. Experiments on 2.5D/3D IC benchmarks show that HLWalk achieves remarkable wall-clock speedup and better accuracy across settings.

papers.title: Verifiable Logical-Physical Contracts for Refactored On-Die Power Control Circuitry
papers.abstract: Recent literature allows independent hardware experiments to occupy a single die for scalable and cost-efficient silicon prototyping. Within this framework, specialized hardware functions including low-power control mechanisms can be offered as reusable on-die microservices. However, this requires well-defined contracts connecting digital requests to physical behavior. We present a checkable logical-physical contract formulation including a physical contract model describing service completion between client and provider through formally verified digital guarantees and physically validated completion conditions. We introduce Lightswitch, a proof-of-concept on-die power control microservice. We assess post-layout designs in TSMC 28nm and demonstrate how checkable contracts provide formal guarantees.

papers.title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

papers.title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
papers.abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

papers.title: A Systematic Method of GPU Verification on Subsystem Modelling
papers.abstract: ARM Fast Model is a software modelling system for simulating multiple systems IPs integrated in a subsystem. Fast Model allows customer to run whole software stack as early as system IPs' specification is just ready. In this paper, we talk about a systematic method to enable GPU modelling and make whole system software stacks executable for both CPU and GPU in the integrated modelling environment, and eventually the major GPU IP can be verified. With our solution, we can directly run commercial benchmarks like Antutu and GFX Bench in Android target system with underlying ARM Fast Model mobile subsystem support. This was unbelievable in the past due to 3D rendering simulation for GPU verification is very slow. We also introduce some special techniques to improve performance. Eventually the whole software stack can directly work on real hardware without any changes as soon as the first tape-out is ready.

papers.title: Selective ROM Weight Storage for Responsive LLM Control on Edge Robots
papers.abstract: Edge robots increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for complex tasks, demanding efficient inference alongside timely control. Limited memory capacity constrains model deployment, while repeated weight transfers during decoding compete with activations and KV cache for external bandwidth. Sequential generation of robot actions further delays decisions and periodic control on shared hardware. We present a hybrid memory architecture with heterogeneous scheduling to address these bottlenecks jointly. Banked ROM stores selected fixed weights and supplies a standard compute array through a dedicated datapath. LPDDR retains the remaining weights and mutable state, preserving model flexibility. Coordinated operand delivery and preemption at output slice boundaries accelerate inference while limiting interference with periodic control. A structured decision interface scores candidate phases in a single forward pass, avoiding sequential token generation for routine choices. Together, these mechanisms improve memory service, compute access, and decision execution for edge robotic workloads. Experiments with Qwen3-8B achieve a peak decode speedup of 1.56$\times$ and reduce P99 task response time by a factor of approximately 227.27$\times$, while completing 100.00\% of the tested grasping and transport tasks.

papers.title: APUF-SNG: A Low-Cost Arbiter-PUF Stochastic Number Generator with Tunable Output Probability
papers.abstract: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes numerical values as probabilistic bit-streams and enables arithmetic operations using simple logic gates, offering a promising paradigm for low- cost, fault-tolerant, and highly parallel computation. However, the accuracy and efficiency of SC systems depend on the quality of the stochastic number generator (SNG). Conventional SNGs rely on pseudo-random or quasi-random generators, whose deterministic nature introduces periodicity, correlation, and bias, limiting achievable accuracy and robustness. This paper proposes a low- cost arbiter physical unclonable function (APUF)-based SNG that operates in near-metastable delay conditions to generate true- random stochastic bit-streams with controllable output probabilities. By selecting input challenges that drive the path delay difference toward a target value, the resulting output probability is governed by intrinsic device noise, eliminating the need for conventional random-number generators and comparator-based SNGs. The proposed design inherits the low hardware overhead and statistical independence properties of the APUF structure. A probabilistic model and a challenge selection method are developed to characterize and control the stochastic behavior. An 8-stage APUF-SNG matches the 1% mean absolute error of state- of-the-art true-random SNGs at 1024-bit streams and occupies 116{\mu}m^2 in 45nm, 2.5x and 7x smaller than the TRNG-based and Sobol-based generator designs, respectively.

papers.title: VEGA: A Scalable Software-Hardware Co-design for Genome Alignment using RVV Extension
papers.abstract: Dynamic programming (DP)-based genome sequence analysis is fundamental to computational genomics, but it remains computationally intensive as genomic data volumes continue to outpace Moore's Law. Existing hardware accelerators often sacrifice programmability and scalability across diverse alignment algorithms. In this work, we present VEGA, a scalable software-hardware co-design that accelerates genome alignment using RISC-V Vector extensions. VEGA introduces specialized vector instructions and three key innovations: a Forefront Stationary dataflow that minimizes off-chip memory access, intersequence parallelism that maximizes SIMD lane utilization, and custom ISA extensions that accelerate core alignment operations. Evaluations show that VEGA achieves up to 15.1x and 9.7x speedups for Edit Distance and Smith-Waterman algorithms over the Ara2-RVV vector baseline, sustaining 10.2x and 6.7x gains for 10kbp sequences. Post-synthesis results indicate only 1.0% area overhead compared to a standard RISC-V core, with performance-per-area efficiency rivaling specialized ASICs. VEGA thus achieves a balanced advancement in efficiency, programmability, and scalability for genome sequence alignment.

papers.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincar\'e phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.

papers.title: CXL Coherence Writes Back What Surviving Hosts See, Leaving Flushes Only for Ordering
papers.abstract: Hosts that share memory over Compute Express Link (CXL) cache its lines, and a host that crashes loses the lines it has modified and not written back. Designs for such memory stop every host when one crashes, assume stored energy, or flush after each operation. We show that when a crashing host's clients die with it, the flushes a host crash requires are those that keep one line from reaching the memory device before a line it depends on, and not those that make a finished operation durable. The reason is a property that CXL requires of the fabric: a modified line is written back before another host accesses it. Whatever a surviving host has seen is then on the device, and our crash condition lets a crash drop operations that only the crashed host observed. We prove the claim for operations that take effect in a single store, and test it on small instances of models of three published designs, whose operations store several times. A lock table needs no flush to keep the locks of surviving hosts. A persistent hash index keeps every operation a survivor has observed, and in two workloads it writes fewer than half as many lines to the device as its published code does. An allocator's flush of each new reference is neither sufficient nor necessary for the survivors' safety: the allocator lacks ordering flushes, one of them when a reference changes hands.

papers.title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
papers.abstract: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.
